scope_note: SG-RESTRICTED-NONPRESCRIPTION-SALES after corrections following the V10G audit. The scheduled listed chemical product duties are still placed on the regulated seller, but the section now teaches that 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes unlawful disclosure of logbook information, or refusing the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement, a prohibited act for the seller or an employee or agent, with the civil and criminal consequences in 842(c), and that 21 CFR 1314.45(a) says the information shall be disclosed as appropriate (worked example [5] no longer says may). The excepted-preparation teaching is rebuilt around a dated finding: as of 2026-09-16 no exception under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 was found in 105 CMR 700.000, 105 CMR 720-726 or 247 CMR; s. 4(3) requires a federal exception, and 21 U.S.C. 811(g) and 21 CFR 1308.21-1308.35 allow none for a nonprescription preparation (and an opium-containing preparation is a narcotic drug), so no controlled-substance preparation can currently be sold without a prescription in Massachusetts; the s. 5 terms are taught as what would govern if an exception were ever made, and the combined state-and-federal sale analysis, its decision step, its trap and the worked example resolving to a four-ounce ceiling are removed or rewritten. The mail-order row now cites 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1) and (e)(2)(B), and orientation[14] credits chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018 only with striking the age and identification provisions. New rules: FED-SLCP-LOGBOOK-DISCLOSURE-PROHIBITED-ACTS, FED-CS-PREPARATION-EXCLUSION-EXEMPTION-CATEGORIES and MA-CS-S4-NO-CURRENT-EXCEPTIONS. MA-Q-0121 left the practice links because its premise, a preparation already confirmed to qualify for the s. 4 exception, cannot occur today. Scope gate: the same 14 actionable signals as the previous freeze are declined, for the reasons recorded there: two are records this section replaced (MA-EXCEPTED-CS-SALE, MA-HYPODERMIC-SALE) and the rest belong to schedule placement, administration, refills, controlled-substance theft and loss, the general readily-retrievable definition, or prescription dispensing.
